title: Duryodhana Resolves to Imprison Krishna
subtitle: Bhishma Departs in Anger
story:
Duryodhana listened to the debate over Krishna's welcome, and when he finally spoke, he agreed with Vidura on one point alone: that Janardana could never be separated from the Pandavas. "All that Vidura has said about Krishna has been truly said," he declared. "Janardana is greatly devoted to the Pandavas and can never be separated from them. The diverse kinds of wealth proposed to be bestowed upon him ought never to be bestowed. Kesava is, of course, not unworthy of our worship — but both time and place are against it, for on receiving our worship he will very likely think that we are worshipping him out of fear. It is my certain conviction that an intelligent Kshatriya must not do that which may bring disgrace upon him. The large-eyed Krishna deserves the most reverential worship of the three worlds. It is quite out of place, therefore, to give him anything now — for war having been decided upon, it should never be put off by hospitality."

So much for the gifts. What replaced them was worse. The Grandsire, Bhishma, answered in his deep old voice: "Worshipped or not worshipped, Janardana never becomes angry. None, however, can treat him with disrespect, for Kesava is not contemptible. Whatever he purposes to do is incapable of being frustrated by anybody, by every means in his power. Do without hesitation what Krishna of mighty arms says, and bring about peace with the Pandavas through Vasudeva as the means. Janardana, possessed of a virtuous soul, will say what is consistent with religion and profit. It behooves you, therefore, with all your friends, to tell him only what is agreeable to him."

Duryodhana's answer came like a blow. "O Grandsire, I can by no means live by sharing this swelling prosperity of mine with the Pandavas. Listen — this is a great resolution which I have formed. I will imprison Janardana, who is the refuge of the Pandavas. He will come here tomorrow morning; and when he is confined, the Vrishnis and the Pandavas — aye, the whole earth — will submit to me. What may be the means for accomplishing it, so that Janardana may not guess our purpose, and so that no danger may overtake us, it behooves you to say."

A silence fell over the hall. Even Dhritarashtra, who had yielded to his son in so much, recoiled. Hearing these fearful words about imprisoning Krishna, the king and all his counsellors were very much pained and became deeply afflicted. "O ruler of men," he said to Duryodhana, "never say this again. This is not immemorial custom. Hrishikesa comes here as an ambassador. He is, besides, related to us and dear to us. He has done us no wrong. How then does he deserve imprisonment?"

But the old king's protest only released the older man's wrath. Bhishma rose from his seat. "This wicked son of yours, O Dhritarashtra, has his hour come," he said. "He chooses evil, not good, though entreated by his well-wishers. You also follow in the wake of this wicked wretch of sinful surroundings, who treads a thorny path, setting at naught the words of his well-wisher. This exceedingly wicked son of yours, with all his counsellors, coming in contact with Krishna of unstained acts, will be destroyed in a moment. I dare not listen to the words of this sinful and wicked wretch that has abandoned all virtue."

And having said this, the aged chief of the Bharata race, Bhishma of unbaffled prowess, inflamed with rage, rose and left that place — the assembly staring after him, the blind king stricken, the prince unmoved, and the plan to imprison the ambassador left standing in the middle of the hall like a storm that had not yet broken.
reflection: Duryodhana's resolution turns diplomacy into a siege: he will imprison the ambassador who came to make peace, confident that holding one man will bend the whole earth. Bhishma's rage is the measure of the folly — he walks out rather than listen, naming the ruin he already sees coming.
next_story_tease: At dawn, Krishna would enter Hastinapura and walk into the middle of that broken council to meet Dhritarashtra.
hero_scene: Bhishma, tall and white-bearded, rises in rage from the Kuru assembly and turns his back on Duryodhana, who sits flushed and defiant, while Dhritarashtra bows his head in pain.
visual_elements: Duryodhana declaring his resolution before the assembly
Bhishma rising in rage from his seat
